title: The Shrinkage Estimator Hiding in Your Denoiser

body:
A statistician holding five thousand noisy effect estimates and an engineer training a text-to-image model are, at the level of the estimator, computing the same object: the posterior mean of a latent quantity under a prior neither of them has written down and neither intends to. Both reach it by the same route, differentiating the log of the marginal density of the observed data. The statistician calls this Tweedie's formula and treats it with well-earned suspicion, having spent seventy years cataloguing the ways it misbehaves. The engineer calls it the $\epsilon$-prediction objective and treats it as an implementation detail.

The identity is exact and it is old. What it comes with is a warning label that only one of the two fields has read. Those failure modes did not stop being true when the marginal density started being estimated by a U-Net, and the diffusion literature has largely rediscovered them under other names — blurry one-step outputs, memorization at small dataset sizes, guidance that produces images no posterior would produce — without connecting them to the seventy years of theory that predicted each one.

## Why the identity is suddenly load-bearing

Empirical Bayes is in an unusually active phase. David Blei's 2026 IMS Medallion Lecture, [*A Fresh Look at Empirical Bayes*](https://imstat.org/2026/03/31/ims-medallion-lecture-preview-david-blei/), proposes reviving the program under three banners — empirical Bayes via probabilistic symmetries, empirical Bayes with implicit likelihoods through simulation-based inference, and empirical Bayes for combining experimental and observational data. Polson, Sokolov and Zantedeschi answered within weeks with [*An Old Look at Empirical Bayes*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21535), which opens on Lindley's line that there is only one thing worse than a frequentist, and that is an empirical Bayesian, and argues that the computational excuse for the shortcut has expired. Their case study is Tweedie's formula specifically.

At the same time the estimator is being learned rather than constructed. Teh, Jabbour and Polyanskiy showed in [*Solving Empirical Bayes via Transformers*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.09844) that transformers with on the order of 100k parameters, pretrained on synthetic prior–observation pairs, beat nonparametric maximum likelihood on both runtime and validation loss in the Poisson compound-decision problem, including on real data. Cannella, Teh, Han and Polyanskiy supplied the theory at COLT 2026 in [*Universal priors*](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v336/cannella26a.html): there exist priors such that pretraining under them yields near-optimal regret uniformly over test distributions.

Meanwhile, and this is my characterization rather than anyone's claim, diffusion models constitute by a wide margin the largest deployment of an empirical Bayes estimator in the history of statistics, and essentially none of that literature cites Robbins.

## Four lines

Let $\theta \sim g$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$, with $g$ unknown and arbitrary, and let $z \mid \theta \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta, \sigma^2 I)$. Write $\varphi_\sigma$ for the $\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2 I)$ density and

$$f_\sigma(z) = \int \varphi_\sigma(z - \theta), g(d\theta)$$

for the marginal. Differentiating under the integral,

$$\nabla_z f_\sigma(z) = \int \nabla_z \varphi_\sigma(z-\theta), g(d\theta) = \int \frac{\theta - z}{\sigma^2}, \varphi_\sigma(z-\theta), g(d\theta),$$

so that

$$\sigma^2 \nabla_z \log f_\sigma(z) = \int (\theta - z) \frac{\varphi_\sigma(z-\theta) g(d\theta)}{f_\sigma(z)} = \mathbb{E}[\theta \mid z] - z,$$

giving Tweedie's formula:

$$\mathbb{E}[\theta \mid z] = z + \sigma^2 \nabla_z \log f_\sigma(z).$$

Stare at the right-hand side. The prior $g$ does not appear. The Bayes rule — the thing that ought to require knowing $g$ — is a functional of the marginal distribution of data you can actually see. That is the whole trick, and it is also the whole danger, because you have traded a hard estimation problem (recover $g$ by deconvolution) for one that looks easier and is not: estimate a density's log-gradient well enough that plugging it in is safe.

[Efron](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1198/jasa.2011.tm11181) named the two routes *f-modeling* and *g-modeling*: estimate the marginal and differentiate it, or estimate the prior and integrate against it. Both are legitimate; they fail differently. The formula itself traces to Robbins' [1956 Berkeley Symposium paper](https://projecteuclid.org/proceedings/berkeley-symposium-on-mathematical-statistics-and-probability/Proceedings-of-the-Third-Berkeley-Symposium-on-Mathematical-Statistics-and/Chapter/An-Empirical-Bayes-Approach-to-Statistics/bsmsp/1200501653), who credited it to Maurice Tweedie and gave the discrete analogue for Poisson data, $\mathbb{E}[\theta \mid x] = (x+1) f(x+1)/f(x)$, which needs no derivative at all.

Differentiate once more. Since $\nabla^2_z \log f_\sigma$ is the Jacobian of the score,

$$\mathrm{Cov}(\theta \mid z) = \sigma^2 I + \sigma^4 \nabla^2_z \log f_\sigma(z),$$

which means the Jacobian of the Bayes denoiser $D(z) = \mathbb{E}[\theta\mid z]$ satisfies $J_D(z) = \mathrm{Cov}(\theta \mid z)/\sigma^2$. The denoiser's own derivative *is* its posterior covariance, up to scale. Two consequences follow immediately and I will use both: you get uncertainty quantification for free, and you get a falsifiable structural constraint, because $J_D$ must be symmetric and positive semidefinite.

## What the sampler is actually doing

Take the standard forward process $x_t = \alpha_t x_0 + \sigma_t \varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)$. Divide through: $x_t/\alpha_t = x_0 + (\sigma_t/\alpha_t)\varepsilon$. This is the Gaussian sequence model above, verbatim, with prior $g = \mathrm{law}(x_0)$ and noise scale $\sigma_t/\alpha_t$. Tweedie gives

$$\mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x_t] = \frac{1}{\alpha_t}\Big(x_t + \sigma_t^2 \nabla_{x_t} \log p_t(x_t)\Big).$$

The training objective closes the loop. Minimizing $\mathbb{E}|\varepsilon - \varepsilon_\phi(x_t,t)|^2$ over an unconstrained $\varepsilon_\phi$ has minimizer $\varepsilon^\star(x_t,t) = \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon \mid x_t] = -\sigma_t \nabla \log p_t(x_t)$ — the identity [Vincent](https://direct.mit.edu/neco/article-abstract/23/7/1661/7677) established in 2011 between denoising autoencoder training and score matching, three years before anyone was sampling images with it. So [DDPM](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2020/hash/4c5bcfec8584af0d967f1ab10179ca4b-Abstract.html)'s noise-prediction network is trained to be, at optimum, exactly the posterior mean; the score is a reparametrization of it and neither is a representation of $g$.

There is one structural difference from the classical setting worth naming, and I think it is the interesting one. Classical empirical Bayes has a single tuning problem: how much to smooth the marginal, equivalently how much shrinkage to apply. It has no principled answer. Diffusion sidesteps the question by refusing to pick — it solves the empirical Bayes problem at *every* noise level and traverses the family. As $\sigma \to \infty$, $\mathbb{E}[\theta\mid z] \to \mathbb{E}[\theta]$, total shrinkage to the prior mean; as $\sigma \to 0$ the estimator becomes the identity and shrinks nothing. Sampling is a walk down that one-parameter path, handing off from a heavily shrunk estimate to a barely shrunk one. Annealing is not an optimization trick bolted onto a Bayes rule; it is what makes an otherwise intractable estimation problem behave.

## A two-point prior, worked

Nothing exposes the shape of the estimator like a prior small enough to compute by hand. Take $g = 0.9,\delta_0 + 0.1,\delta_5$ and $\sigma = 1$, so $f(z) = 0.9,\varphi(z) + 0.1,\varphi(z-5)$. Prior mean $0.5$, prior variance $2.25$.

| $z$ | $\mathbb{E}[\theta\mid z]$ | $\mathbb{E}[\theta\mid z] - z$ | $\mathrm{Var}(\theta\mid z)$ |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1.0 | 0.0003 | −1.000 | 0.0015 |
| 2.0 | 0.045 | −1.955 | 0.224 |
| 2.5 | 0.500 | −2.000 | 2.250 |
| 3.0 | 2.876 | −0.124 | 6.109 |
| 3.5 | 4.714 | **+1.214** | 1.348 |
| 4.0 | 4.975 | **+0.975** | 0.123 |
| 5.0 | 5.000 | −0.0002 | 0.0008 |

Three things in that table are worth more than the sum of their parts.

The correction is signed and non-monotone. At $z=2$ the rule pulls the estimate down by $1.96$; at $z=3.5$ it pushes it *up* by $1.21$. Tweedie is called a shrinkage formula and here it expands. Anyone whose mental picture of empirical Bayes is James–Stein pulling everything toward a grand mean is carrying an image that holds only when $g$ is Gaussian, in which case the rule is linear. For every other prior the "shrinkage" is whatever $\nabla \log f$ says, and $\nabla \log f$ points uphill in the marginal, which near a low-density trough means away from where you came from.

At $z = 2.5$ the two likelihoods are exactly equal, so the posterior equals the prior: mean $0.5$, variance $2.25$. The observation, sitting halfway between the two atoms, has told you nothing. And the estimate $0.5$ is a value the prior assigns zero mass. This is not a defect — it is the definition of a posterior mean under a multimodal posterior, and it is precisely why single-step diffusion outputs look like superpositions rather than samples. Blur is the correct answer to the question MMSE asks.

Finally, at $\sigma = 1$ the identity $\mathrm{d}\mathbb{E}[\theta\mid z]/\mathrm{d}z = 1 + (\log f)''(z) = \mathrm{Var}(\theta \mid z)$ holds exactly, and both peak at $6.25$ near $z \approx 2.94$. The estimator is $6.25$-Lipschitz there: maximally sensitive exactly where the posterior is most uncertain. The marginal density at that point is $0.0096$, about $2.7%$ of its value at the mode. The region where the plug-in rule most amplifies error is the region where you have the least data to estimate it from. That sentence is the entire case against naive f-modeling, and it does not improve in higher dimensions.

## What to do with this

**Use the model you already have as an estimator.** A trained diffusion model is a nonparametric estimate of $\nabla \log f_\sigma$ at a continuum of bandwidths. You can apply it as a shrinkage operator to problems that have nothing to do with generation, without ever positing a prior. [Noise2Score](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.07009) makes exactly this move for image denoising under arbitrary exponential-family noise, and [Raphan and Simoncelli](https://direct.mit.edu/neco/article-abstract/23/2/374/7627/Least-Squares-Estimation-Without-Priors-or) had already worked out how to generalize Tweedie beyond Gaussian likelihoods.

**Test the symmetry.** This is my recommendation rather than anything in the literature, but the mathematics is not negotiable: if $D$ is the posterior mean of *any* distribution under Gaussian noise, then $D(z) = z + \sigma^2\nabla \log f$ is a gradient field and $J_D$ is symmetric. Two directional derivatives suffice.

```python
import torch
def symmetry_gap(D, x, n=8):          # D: denoiser, x: single noisy input
    gaps = []
    for _ in range(n):
        u, v = torch.randn_like(x), torch.randn_like(x)
        _, Ju = torch.func.jvp(D, (x,), (u,))
        _, Jv = torch.func.jvp(D, (x,), (v,))
        num = (v * Ju).sum() - (u * Jv).sum()      # v'Ju - u'Jv, exactly 0 if symmetric
        gaps.append((num / (Ju.norm() * v.norm() + 1e-8)).abs())
    return torch.stack(gaps).mean()
```

A gap that is not small means your denoiser is not the posterior mean of anything, and the trace-based uncertainty estimate you were about to compute from it has no interpretation.

**Stop calling guided outputs posterior means.** Classifier-free guidance forms $D_\varnothing + w(D_c - D_\varnothing)$ with $w > 1$. That is an extrapolation outside the convex hull of two posterior means, and it is not $\mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x_t, c]$ under any prior — the reason it improves samples is precisely that it stops being one. Expect the symmetry diagnostic to fail on guided denoisers by construction, and do not reason about their outputs with Bayes-rule intuitions.

**Read the arrow in the other direction too.** If you are hand-rolling NPMLE for a compound-decision problem, the transformer results above are worth twenty minutes of your attention.

## Where it breaks

The plug-in step is the weak joint, and Efron's [*Two Modeling Strategies*](https://projecteuclid.org/journals/statistical-science/volume-29/issue-2/Two-Modeling-Strategies-for-Empirical-Bayes-Estimation/10.1214/13-STS455.pdf) is the honest accounting: f-modeling requires differentiating an estimated log-density, which is unstable wherever the density is small, which is exactly the tails and troughs where interesting cases live. The two-point example makes the mechanism visible in one dimension; nothing about $d = 10^5$ helps.

Polson and coauthors push further, and I think their objection is underweighted. A smoothed or regularized score need not be the score of any marginal arising from any prior — the plug-in estimate can be *incoherent*, a function that no Bayesian model implies. [Datta and Polson](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.05823) make this sharp in the tractable case: in exponential-family models a polynomial log-marginal of degree $k \ge 3$ cannot arise from any valid prior, while the quadratic case corresponds exactly to a Gaussian prior. Fitting a flexible $\log \hat f$ and reading a Bayes rule off it is therefore not a benign approximation; the object you get may lie outside the model class entirely. Whether the same pathology afflicts a U-Net's score is, to my knowledge, unstudied — but the common claim that a diffusion model "implicitly represents a prior over images" should be read as a conjecture rather than a restatement of Tweedie.

Then there is the awkward fact that nonparametric score estimation in the dimensionality of images should be hopeless, and empirically is not. [Kadkhodaie, Guth, Simoncelli and Mallat](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.02557) showed that two networks trained on non-overlapping subsets memorize at small $N$ and converge to nearly the same score function at large $N$, which localizes the explanation in architectural inductive bias rather than in estimation. The empirical Bayes framing therefore describes the *estimand* exactly and the *estimator* not at all. Classical regret guarantees — [Jiang and Zhang](https://projecteuclid.org/journals/annals-of-statistics/volume-37/issue-4/General-maximum-likelihood-empirical-Bayes-estimation-of-normal-means/10.1214/08-AOS638.full) for GMLEB, [Koenker and Mizera](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/01621459.2013.869224) for the convex-optimization NPMLE — live in a regime with no known bridge to this one, and the COLT universal-priors theorem is likewise a classical-setting result. As far as I can tell nobody has connected them, and I would treat any claim that diffusion "inherits" empirical Bayes optimality as unsupported.

Finally, empirical Bayes uncertainty has always been the sore point, since the data are used twice — much of Efron's [*Bayes, Oracle Bayes and Empirical Bayes*](https://projecteuclid.org/journals/statistical-science/volume-34/issue-2/Bayes-Oracle-Bayes-and-Empirical-Bayes/10.1214/18-STS674.full) is repair work on exactly this. The posterior covariance identity above is exact for the true $f$ and contains no term for the gap between $\hat f$ and $f$. Anyone reading calibrated error bars off a denoiser Jacobian is reporting the uncertainty of a model that is assumed correct.

- Efron, *Tweedie's Formula and Selection Bias*, JASA 106(496):1602–1614, 2011. [tandfonline.com](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1198/jasa.2011.tm11181) — the modern reference statement, the exponential-family generalization, and the connection to James–Stein and to regression to the mean.

- Efron, *Bayes, Oracle Bayes and Empirical Bayes*, Statistical Science 34(2):177–201, 2019. - Vincent, *A Connection Between Score Matching and Denoising Autoencoders*, Neural Computation 23(7):1661–1674, 2011. [direct.mit.edu](https://direct.mit.edu/neco/article-abstract/23/7/1661/7677) — the identity that makes the diffusion objective a score estimator; predates the generative application entirely.

[direct.mit.edu](https://direct.mit.edu/neco/article-abstract/23/2/374/7627/Least-Squares-Estimation-Without-Priors-or) — Tweedie generalized to arbitrary known likelihoods; the reference to reach for when your noise is not Gaussian.
- Ho, Jain, Abbeel, *Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models*, NeurIPS 2020. [proceedings.neurips.cc](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2020/hash/4c5bcfec8584af0d967f1ab10179ca4b-Abstract.html) — worth rereading with the empirical Bayes lens; the $\epsilon$-parametrization is a Tweedie reparametrization.
- Kim, Ye, *Noise2Score: Tweedie's Approach to Self-Supervised Image Denoising without Clean Images*, NeurIPS 2021. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.07009) — the cleanest demonstration of using the identity as an estimator rather than as a sampler.
- Kadkhodaie, Guth, Simoncelli, Mallat, *Generalization in Diffusion Models Arises from Geometry-Adaptive Harmonic Representations*, ICLR 2024 (Outstanding Paper). [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.02557) — the disjoint-training-set convergence experiment; the strongest evidence that inductive bias, not estimation theory, explains what works.
- Polson, Sokolov, Zantedeschi, *An Old Look at Empirical Bayes*, arXiv:2605.21535, May 2026. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21535) — the coherence objection to plug-in Tweedie, written as a reply to Blei's Medallion Lecture; the most useful recent skepticism.
- Datta, Polson, *Polynomial Log-Marginals and Tweedie's Formula: When Is Bayes Possible?*, arXiv:2509.05823, 2025. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.05823) — the coherence question answered exactly for polynomial log-marginals; the crispest statement of what f-modeling can silently violate.
- Teh, Jabbour, Polyanskiy, *Solving Empirical Bayes via Transformers*, arXiv:2502.09844, 2025. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.09844); and Cannella, Teh, Han, Polyanskiy, *Universal Priors*, COLT 2026. [proceedings.mlr.press](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v336/cannella26a.html) — small pretrained transformers beating NPMLE, and the regret theory that explains why.
